column2: Yes.
Charles Allan Bint.

The examining board to rate the candidates consisted of a representative of the department, a representative of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League, and the civil sendee commission's supervising examiner, Mr. E. J. Hellyer, principal of the

column1: Questions

Dunnville high school. Mr. R. S. Colter, barrister, of Cayuga, Ontario, was selected by the department to represent them in the examination, and the Legion was represented by Mr. G. E. Battle, president of the Dunnville branch.

Since the examination it has been ascertained that the representative of the department was not, as was expected, an officer of the department, which would have been in accordance with the usual practice. Therefore the department has been requested in future examinations for this class of position, to have as its representative either an official of the department or an officer of a military unit, preferably the one in connection with which the vacancy occurs.

He did not feel disposed to have the title drawn in the son's name. I have known this family since I was a boy, and my memory is that the old gentleman was about eighty years of age. 1087295,ca.proc.d.1936-03-25.5.1.7,1936-03-25,ba7c8691-5f1c-4bc4-9ec1-82c0a828db16,ca.m.1501,Mr. QUELCH:,,SOLDIER SETTLEMENT ACT,EXTENSION OP TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES,,I should like to support

the bill, but before doing so may I point out, as other hon. members have done, that although the measure represents a step in the right direction it does not begin to meet the needs of soldier settlers. Last fall when I interviewed the superintendent of the soldier settlement board in Calgary he said he was puzzled because he had not received applications from my constituency. I pointed out to him that the reason was obvious, namely that in the majority of cases the soldier settlers in the south-eastern part of Acadia were in such a hopeless position that they would be unable to repay their indebtedness to the board even if extensions were made indefinitely.

About the time the war ended the soldier settlement board was put into operation and field supervisors were appointed for the purpose of advising and reestablishing returned soldiers. At that time the dominion government had information from their engineers to the effect that the drought areas were unsuitable for settlers. In spite of that fact, however, the supervisors helped a number of soldiers to reestablish themselves in the drought areas, and for that reason the government incurred a direct liability. Although the land had already been condemned as unsuitable, many returned soldiers were established in these areas, and to-day they find themselves in a hopeless position. They have lost what little capital they had and are totally unable to repay their indebtedness. Surely it is the responsibility of the government to reestablish those men in areas in which they might have a chance to succeed. I would urge upon the minister that he make a thorough investigation into the whole problem with a view to a reduction of interest, a revaluation of land, and an extension for at least five years of the dollar for dollar bonus. After five years of depression and low prices the returned men even in the better districts are finding themselves in a precarious position.

column2: That is a substantial

column1: number indeed, considering conditions in the province of Alberta in the last four or five years. I doubt whether this would be the proper time to consider the hon. member's suggestion of further reductions in interest and principal. During the last fifteen or sixteen years, since the soldier settlement scheme was embarked upon, there have been very substantial reductions covering a considerable period of years. In 1922 legislation was passed granting exemption of interest in arrears, and the amount involved was over $10,000,000. In 1925 provision was made for a revaluation of live stock, and a reduction was made in the value of live stock of almost $3,000,000, covering soldier settlers throughout Canada. In 1927 there was a land revaluation, involving a total of $7,500,000. In 1930 legislation was passed providing for a reduction in principal and interest over the whole scheme, involving a sum of $11,300,000. So, during the period that this scheme has been in operation substantial reductions have been made in the obligations of the soldier settlers. Furthermore, when the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed returned soldier settlers, although their debt was to the crown, were brought under the provisions of that measure.

In reply to my hon. friend's suggestion that a two year extension is not sufficient, as I indicated the other day when we were discussing the resolution, if conditions at the expiration of two years warrant a further extension, it will require only a simple amendment to the act, but as my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) pointed out in the debate the other day, if you now make the period five years, the inevitable tendency will be for the soldier settlers to postpone making payments until nearly the end of the period of grace. So, taking it all together, after a very full discussion with the officers of my department, I think a two year extension is probably the wisest at the present time. I am quite aware of the fact that the particular district in Alberta from which my hon. friend from Acadia (Mr. Quelch) comes, has had serious reverses over a period of years. But the history of that district, which I know fairly well, having handled grain from it for a great many years when I was with the United Grain Growers, is that it has its periods of good times and its periods of bad times, and

while everyone in the house desires, I am sure, to extend the fullest possible sympathy and support to the returned soldier settler, I think on the whole the legislation before us will achieve what we have in view.

One other fact that should be kept in mind-and it has been brought to my attention already in the last few months-is that there are on farms throughout Canada to-day many returned soldiers who secured their farms independently of the soldier settlement scheme altogether, and they have had none of these benefits which have accrued to the soldier settlers under the various provisions that I enumerated a moment ago. If we extended the provisions as far as my hon. friend suggests, perhaps these other soldier settlers might have some claim upon us. My hon. friend can rest assured that the administration of the soldier settlement scheme will be as fair and reasonable as possible, and if at the end of two years we find it necessary to make a further extension I am quite certain that this parliament will gladly make it.

dian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, of the net credit balance resulting from transactions by Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, in respect of coarse grains grown in the year 1930. There were four different pools in Saskatchewan and Manitoba; there were no pools in Alberta having to do with coarse grains. The four pools in Saskatchewan and Manitoba had to do with the marketing of oats, barley, flax and rye; these pools were finally handled through Mr. McFarland, as .the representative of the banks, I think, who were financing the pools in their operations, in such a manner as to dispose of these grains, and the amounts that are now in the accounts that were guaranteed by the government are to be returned to the wheat pools to be handled by them in such manner as will be provided in the act. paucity of information which the minister offers on this resolution. Whether it is the settled policy of the government not to supply information on resolutions I do not know, but judging from what was said yesterday apparently it is. Now the rule is clear, and-I speak only for myself-I propose to see that it is observed. We are entitled to this information. It may take a long time to get it but we are entitled to it. One thing we are not entitled to do is to make long speeches on questions of policy. That is the objection I urged last year and the Prime Minister now admits that it is a sound view. It took five sittings to deal with the relief resolution last year though it might have been passed in a little while if speeches had not been made on everything in the world but the resolution itself. I propose to confine myself to this resolution and its terms, and I must asik that the information requested be put on Hansard in order that the public who are watching this matter may be properly informed.

The first question is: Why was this matter not disposed of long ago? It will be recalled that the legislation of last session provided that the Canadian wheat pool should take over from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, the stocks of grain they had on hand and pay for them. These grains belonged to the Canadian Wheat Producers Limited and not to the government of Canada or to the wheat board. But it was thought desirable, not by the government of the day but by a committee which was composed of members from both sides of the house, that the wheat should actually be placed in the
Wheat Board

possession and under the control of the wheat board. To that end the legislation provided that they would take it over. To take it over meant that they had to assume at the bank the obligation which the Canadian Wheat Producers Limited was carrying under the guarantee of the government. That is the position. That is, Mr. McFarland was not appointed to the position of manager of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers by the government; he was appointed by that corporation, and I think the hon. minister is right when he says that undoubtedly the appointment met with the approval of the banks.

There was, then, when this wheat act came into force last year, a quantity of wheat in the possession of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited; they had borrowed the money from the bank to buy the grain and pay for it; and the government had guaranteed the payments to the bank of the money that had been secured for the purpose of making the purchase. Included in that wheat was a quantity of grain that the wheat pools had owned in 1930 and that had been utilized, as the other grains had, in connection with the operations that were carried on. They pointed out that part of that grain had been bought at a price of seventy cents per bushel, part of it at a lesser price, and that initial payments had been made of fifty-five cents and of, I think, some larger sum and lesser sums. They asked as a condition of turning over their grain that they should receive payment on the basis of sixty cents a bushel for the whole of the grain that was to be taken over by the board and not paid for. When the order in council was passed-and reference has been made to it-it provided that they were to be paid that sum of money plus reasonable expenses as certified by auditors. The order in council was passed in September, 1935. The press carried long statements that advances were to be made to the farmers of this country on the eve of an election, to make it appear that some effort was being made to influence them with respect to this matter. That was not the fact at all. The fact is that, not the wheat board but the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited were going to issue cheques to their customers at the rate of sixty cents per bushel, and indeed had taken steps to do so.

That is the position; that is, that the people who were divesting themselves of property and ownership in their wheat asked that, when the obligation that had been incurred in the purchase of it was being taken over by the wheat board, provision should be made for
fMr. Bennett.]

these quantities of grain that had come into their possession at various prices; that it should be averaged at sixty cents per bushel, and that those who had received fifty-five cents should receive the difference between that and sixty cents. I will read it again. It must be remembered that the reason this order in council was passed was that the law said that no agreement was binding as between the wheat board and the wheat pools until it was agreed to by order in council. After setting out the agreement that had been reached between the wheat pools and the wheat board this order in council then goes on in these words:

Now, therefore. His Excellency the Administrator in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, is pleased to approve the terms of acquisition set out in the aforesaid letters and they are hereby approved accordingly.

Let me say accordingly, that had the order in council ended at ""accordingly,"" no doubt would have arisen in anyone's mind that approval by the government was given to the agreement which had been entered into apparently between the wheat board and the pool organization. This agreement could not become an effective agreement until it was approved by the government of Canada.
Now, these words were added. I say ""added"" advisedly:
Subject to the amount referred to in paragraph (b) page 2 hereof being verified by auditors certificates.

Report approved-not the order in council, but the
Wheat Board
report upon which all orders in council are based. It says that the terms of acquisition
-are hereby approved accordingly, subject to the amount referred to in paragraph (b) page two hereof being verified by auditors' certificates.

That was after Mr. Hunter had seen me in Toronto; for as the hon. gentleman said a moment ago, I was in Toronto, and the report which Mr. Hunter brought down, because of the difficulty of getting together men scattered all over the country, was signed by five members, and the words that were added to the report-not to the order in council, because the report precedes the order in council-were these: This to be verified by auditors' certificates. Why? I do not think any president of the privy council to whom the report of the Minister of Finance was submitted would have done otherwise than say, when you are dealing with a large sum such as this, that it should be verified by the auditors' certificate. Why? Because it was known to the committee that considered these matters last year that in every instance the auditors' reports had been made from week to week and from month to month; these auditors' reports were sent to the Department of Finance, and upon them the action was taken that was reviewed by the committee last year.

Now the hon. gentleman says: I want to do it this way, not in any hole in the corner way, behind closed doors. Why that gratuitous insult to a committee that dealt with these matters and on which were members of his own party, Colonel Ralston being one, and the Hon. Charles Stewart another, two exministers of the crown? They were sitting upon that committee when the provision of section 7, subsection (f) was under consideration, that is as to the terms under which the wheat was to be acquired, and this section was agreed to by everyone in that committee. But more, the bill came back to this house and received the unanimous endorsation of this house, the unanimous support of the house. Let us see what section 7, paragraph (f), says:

Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, to acquire from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council, all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada has given a guarantee.

Of course it did not cover anything but wheat. It covered wheat alone. That was the language of the section. And the report made by the Minister of Finance-which in view of the reference that has been made to it the hon. gentleman will also table in order
that there may be no question about it

that report upon which the order in council in this case was based, was a report that the government approved of the purchase of this wheat from the wheat producers by the Canadian wheat board, and it recites that whereas the wheat board is empowered to acquire wheat from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, and whereas the Minister of Finance reports that they have offered to sell their wheat:

Now, therefore, His Excellency the Administrator in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, is pleased to approve the terms of acquisition set out in the aforesaid letters, and they are hereby approved accordingly, subject to the amount referred to in paragraph (b) page 2 hereof being verified by auditors' certificates.
What is paragraph (b)? It is this:

The Canadian Wheat Board will pay to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited the sum of $8,262,415.37, being the sum total of balances due to the primary producers, and expenses and other charges in connection with the holding and handling of the wheat.

The governor in council, careful of the interests of this country, did not ask his excellency to approve of it as it stood, but said, ""subject to auditors' report."" And because that is done we have listened this afternoon to what I venture to say has never before been heard of in any parliament or any house of commons, an attempt to say that the original of a document has had something written into it in ink, which is not suggested as having been fraudulently done or being a forgery, but because it is written in, it is suggested that it is a circumstance that merits condemnation.

No public men can possibly do business if they are to be subject to implications of that kind, if they are to be a circumstance to be referred to, when we have not access to public records unless they are produced here, and when a minister of the crown says, ""And there it ended,"" and then says that these words were added in writing. If that is to be done, then the rewards of public life are wholly incommensurate with the imputations thus involved. Men value their reputation for honesty and honour and integrity far beyond any implications and suggestions that they would be guilty of endeavouring to add words to an order in council. That meant, if it meant anything, that these words were added under circumstances of a sinister character; for if they were added properly, then they should not have been the subject matter of discussion, inasmuch as they involve a study of the original documents not in the possession of the house.

1087453,ca.proc.d.1936-03-25.6.127,1936-03-25,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH BESPECT TO 1030 WHEAT CROP,,,As my hon. friend from

Yale says, the insinuation was greeted with applause. Has public life sunk to that? Are my colleagues, Mr. Rhodes, who is not in the house, Sir George Perley and others who constituted the council of that day, to be subject to this insinuation, with the applause of members in the chamber? That is the real issue; otherwise there is no purpose in referring to it at all. If the hon. gentleman did not say that he did not say anything. That is the position at this moment.

I put it to the Minister of Justice, I put it to any member of the profession to which he and I belong: Is it open to any other construction than the one I have made, when an original document which I cannot see is referred to and the statement is made, not once but twice, ""Here it ended,"" and then

the further statement made that these words were added in pen and ink, and not by typewriter, and upon that you have a burst of applause. I put it to the hon. gentleman, that means but one thing; there could not have been in the mind of the man who used those words other than one suggestion, and on behalf of my former colleagues I protest and ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice to bring into the house the original report and the original order in council in order to make it perfectly apparent, from the Clerk of the Privy Council, that the document from which he made this copy was the document that went into his custody when the administrator had approved of it and that there had been no alteration or change in it.

Men do not desire to smart under imputations of that kind. It may be a simple and easy thing to jeer and laugh, but some of us are no longer young and we value at least something of the reputation for integrity which we built up in the course of many years-something that is not to be impeached and impugned in the manner in which it has been this afternoon. I was not present; and no member of the legal profession, at least no court of law, would for a single moment permit what has been done; and the Minister of Justice, if he exercises his powers as Minister of Justice of this country, will see to it that immediately, without delay, this house shall have an opportunity to see for itself that there has been no deceit practised on the crown, no fraud practised on anyone, but that the words that were added to the report upon which the order in council was made were words to protect the public interest. And if they were put down in writing instead of in typewriting, it is the usual course with respect to matters of this kind. When it is insinuated that some other course was pursued, I can only say I was not present, and I resent it on behalf of those with whom I have been associated and whose reputation in this country will bear the closest scrutiny by anyone, even by those who applauded the insinuation made this afternoon.

column1: From that there is no report that I can see stating that the amount of $8,262,415.37 is correct or incorrect, except that they say that it does include coarse grains, which was not the purpose of the order in council. The

order in council deals with wheat, and the sum mentioned included coarse grains and expenses. It was for that purpose that the provision was made, as I stated this afternoon at the very beginning of this discussion, that there should be an auditor's report, and there was an auditor's report upon which this legislation is based. There is no reason why there should have been any legislation with respect to this question, none whatever, because I find this afternoon that the statute has not been repealed, and subsection (f) of section 7 provides that they may pay this money to the wheat producers on the basis of this act of last session. With respect to coarse grains there is no provision, and that might have to be the subject matter of legislation. On that point I express no opinion because the matter has not been directed to my attention at the moment. But in dealing with the order in council, which was the order in council that I believed, until this afternoon, was passed, there was no endeavour to deceive or impute fraud to the crown or anyone else. I repeat that as far as this report shows, the amount mentioned in the order in council, which amount was not accepted by the government of the day, but was made subject to investigation and report by the auditors, is a sum that does include coarse grains, and includes them improperly, ais was pointed out by myself; for the language of the order in council does not cover coarse grains. The important point was that there had to be an auditor's report with respect to those items and the .expenses that had been incurred, in order that there might be no question as to the correctness of the amount. I heard this afternoon strong and loud criticisms because the government of the day took steps to provide that before parting with any money with respect to these matters there should be a certificate given to the governor in council by the auditors. But what I am interested in is this. I asked as to the delay, and the minister said the report of the auditors was dated January 25, 1936. It is directed to the Minister of Finance, and perhaps he will inform us now what was the date of his letter of instructions, in order that we may have no misunderstanding on the question of delay. I pointed out the other day in a question to the Prime Minister that much dissatisfaction had been expressed on the part of those entitled to the money that they had not received it weeks and months ago. In view of the instructions referred to in this document we should at least know the date of such instructions, so that there may be no question as to what has caused the delay. I want to deal with the other phases of the resolution after we have disposed of this.

The suggestion was made a number of times during the last half hour that insinuations were made by me in regard to this particular order in council. Now, therefore, His Excellency the Administrator in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, is pleased to approve the terms of acquisition set out in the aforesaid letters, and they are hereby approved accordingly.

I went on to state, Mr. Chairman, that if this order in council had ended there, there would have been no necessity for delay; that the government then in power would have paid out the amount involved, namely $8,262,415.37, and that they would have lost no time in paying it out. But for some reason -and in answer to a suggestion by the leader of the opposition I went on to state the time that that was done-these words were added on:
Subject to the amount referred to in paragraph (b) page 2 hereof being verified by auditors' certificates.
I stated to him that this was the reason for the delay,

the reason, I assume, why his government delayed in the four days before the election, when they had time to make the payment, and in the few days after the election during which they held office. They delayed, apparently, because of the fact that they had put this rider on the order as originally drawn, before it was signed, and before it actually became an order in council. These words made it necessary for his government to get certification from the auditors before any payments were made.

I went on to say that when we came into office and read that order in council with chose words in it we in turn did issue instructions, through the Minister of Finance, to the auditors to have an auditors' statement made. The auditors' statement was made, and was brought down on January 25. We examined it in its particulars before arriving at a conclusion in regard to it, and then as a result of having studied it carefully, and as a result of those findings, we are bringing down legislation to deal with the matter in what we hope will be a conclusive manner.

grains, because I have here at page 35 of the auditors' report, the page from which he was quoting a few moments ago, the statement of the auditors. The amount in this connection to which reference is made in order in council P.C. 3199, is $8,262,415.37. What is referred to in that statement? What happened with regard to this?

As required in your letter of instructions the main purpose of this report and supporting exhibits is to place before you the fullest possible information on. which to base a decision as to what amounts, if any, are due to the primary producers as a result of the operations of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited for the crop of 1930 pool. The amount in this connection referred to in order in council P.C. 3199 is $8,262,415.37 made up as follows:

I shall not read all of the items, but shall be content with giving the totals: Wheat, exhibit A-IV, $6,509,269.36; coarse grains, SS90.658.44; expenses of provincial pool organization for the year 1930-31, $862,487.57, making a total of $8,262,415.37.

I asked the right hon. the leader of the opposition a few minutes ago whether he or his government intended through this order in council to make payments for coarse grains. His answer was that they had not the intention of doing so.

1087536,ca.proc.d.1936-03-25.6.210,1936-03-25,4b5bfbee-1eba-427e-9bad-ddade84ad69e,ca.m.3928,Mr. LAWSON:,,EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH BESPECT TO 1030 WHEAT CROP,,,As soon as the Minister of Agriculture took his seat, following his primary statement to the committee, I endeavoured to obtain the floor, because from the statements he had made I could not help concluding that aspersions had been cast against me, as one of the five who signed the minutes of council and a report upon which an order in council was based, or that in the alternative the clear aspersion was that the former Minister of Finance, one of my colleagues, in fraud of me had added something after my signature had been appended.

I wish to claim privilege in connection with this matter. At this time I merely wish to raise the issue, and to point out that if, after having an opportunity to read Hansard, I find that I am mistaken in my interpretation of my hon. friend's words, I shall have nothing more to say. On the other hand, if I was not mistaken, I want to preserve my right to raise the question before the Speaker of the house. I must confess that I find it difficult to understand that my hon. friend had no intention other
than to explain the delay. If the intention was merely to explain the delay it seems to me that a reading of the clause of the order in council would have served the purpose.

I will ask the hon. gentleman to consider, if his purpose was merely to explain the delay, why in the first place he outlined that there was in existence an order in council which, as he said had been, signed by five members of the council-I think he meant that the report, the minute, had been signed-and then went on to say that a change had been made in ink, and that that change was initialled only by one man who signed the report, namely the former Minister of Finance. I ask him, if his intention was merely to explain the delay, why he was so careful to point out that the amendment was written in with pen and ink. I ask him, if he was only trying to explain the delay, why he started in to impute motives to the former members of the government who were responsible for the order in council because he said from his place, ""Had it been the intention of the government-""
